content: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are defined by significant difficulties in communication and reciprocal social interaction. These challenges can negatively affect relationships within families, increase stress and frustration, and contribute to behaviors that are often described as challenging. Family members of individuals with ASD frequently experience high levels of caregiver stress, a sense of burden, and reduced confidence in their parenting abilities. While psychological interventions have been shown to help both individuals with ASD and their family members by reducing stress, improving mental health, and enhancing coping mechanisms, most research has focused on addressing the needs of either the individual with ASD or their family members separately, rather than both together. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether family therapy, which focuses on improving communication, relationships, and coping strategies, is effective for individuals with ASD and their families. Additionally, the study sought to determine the acceptability of family therapy as a treatment option and, if possible, to assess the economic costs associated with its implementation for this population. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted on January 16, 2017, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and 10 others, as well as three trial registries. Reference lists from existing systematic reviews were also manually searched, and study authors in the field were contacted for additional information. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that evaluated the effectiveness of family therapy for individuals with ASD or their family members. The therapy could be delivered in any format and for any duration, and it was compared to standard care, a wait-list control, or another active psychological intervention. Two authors independently reviewed all titles, abstracts, and full-text reports retrieved during the search. To ensure accuracy, 25% of the materials were also reviewed by a third author. The search process identified 4809 records, of which 37 full-text reports were examined in detail. However, all of these studies were excluded because they did not meet the inclusion criteria. One additional study was identified but remains awaiting classification. The authors concluded that there is a significant lack of research on the effectiveness of family therapy for individuals with ASD. Notably, no randomized controlled trials have been conducted in this area. Further research using rigorous trial designs is urgently needed to determine whether family therapy can improve communication, strengthen relationships, enhance coping mechanisms, and reduce mental health challenges for individuals with ASD and their family members.
